nameStory: Moonflower gets its dreamy name from its spectacular nighttime blooming habit - these large white flowers unfurl in the evening and glow like miniature moons in the darkness. Unlike their morning glory cousins that greet the dawn, moonflowers are night owls that close up when the sun rises, earning them the nickname 'moonvine.'
description: Moonflower is a vigorous climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and stunning pure white trumpet-shaped flowers that can reach 6 inches across. This tropical night-bloomer can climb 10-15 feet in a single growing season, using its twining stems to spiral up fences, trellises, or other plants. In New England, it's grown as an annual since it can't survive our winters, though it may occasionally escape cultivation in warmer microclimates.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large pure white trumpet-shaped blooms up to 6 inches across that open in evening with a sweet, intoxicating fragrance - you can actually watch them spiral open in twilight

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves 3-8 inches long with smooth edges and a soft, velvety texture when young, arranged alternately on twining stems

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Fast-growing climbing vine that twines counterclockwise around supports, reaching 10-15 feet in a season with thick, succulent-feeling stems

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round papery capsules containing 4-6 large dark brown seeds that feel smooth and hard, like small pebbles

idTips.label: Blooming Pattern
idTips.description: Flowers open exclusively in evening and close by mid-morning - if you see white trumpet flowers open during the day, it's likely a different species

habitat: In New England, moonflower is found primarily in cultivated gardens, especially around porches, arbors, and garden trellises where it's planted for evening enjoyment. Occasionally escapes to disturbed areas, roadsides, and fence lines near residential areas, preferring full sun and rich, well-drained soil. Most common in warmer coastal areas and urban heat islands where the growing season is longest.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after last frost, germinating slowly in warming soil. Young seedlings emerge with rounded cotyledons (seed leaves) followed by the first heart-shaped true leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with nightly flower shows from July through August. Vines reach full size and flowers open reliably each evening, releasing their strongest fragrance on humid nights.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until first frost kills the vine. Seed pods mature and dry, turning brown and papery with rattling seeds inside ready for collection.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence in New England - this tropical vine dies completely with frost and must be replanted each year from seed.

funFact: You can literally watch moonflowers open in real-time on summer evenings - the tightly twisted buds spiral open like time-lapse footage over the course of just 10-15 minutes, and the sweet fragrance becomes noticeable from 20 feet away as each flower fully unfurls!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with white-flowered morning glories, but remember the timing trick: moonflowers are 'night shift' workers that open in evening, while morning glories are 'day shift' and close by afternoon. If you see large white trumpet flowers open during sunny daylight hours, you're looking at a morning glory, not a moonflower.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a morning glory, moonflower is actually the opposite - it's an 'evening glory' that belongs to the same plant family but has evolved the reverse blooming schedule. This timing confusion often surprises gardeners who expect it to behave like its daytime cousins.
compareHints: Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red. It also produces the largest flowers in the genus and has the strongest nighttime fragrance, adaptations for attracting night-flying moths rather than daytime butterflies and bees.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
